request:
HL student here, practising Paper 2 quantitative questions. My teacher gave us a made-up company (Source A below) and I've written my calculations and recommendation in my draft (Source B below). The questions were:

(a) Calculate the payback period, average rate of return (ARR) and net present value (NPV) for both options. [8 marks]
(b) Using your results from (a) and the information in Source A, recommend which option Marrowbank Bakery should choose. [10 marks]

Can you check every number in my draft and show the correct working step by step where I've gone wrong (I think my ARR might be too high but I'm not sure why), then give me honest provisional feedback on part (b): what's actually wrong with my reasoning, what I'm missing from Source A, and roughly how far off a top answer it is. Be straight with me rather than just saying "good effort". Also, is NPV really "the most reliable method" like I wrote, or is that something I'd get picked up on?

supplied_texts.title: Source A: Marrowbank Bakery Ltd case data
supplied_texts.text:
Marrowbank Bakery Ltd (fictional case for practice)

Marrowbank Bakery Ltd is a private limited company in a coastal town. It bakes bread and pastries for about 30 cafes and runs one retail shop, employing 14 people. The directors have $150,000 available for investment: $90,000 of retained profit and a $60,000 five-year bank loan at 7% interest, repayable in equal annual instalments starting in Year 1. They are considering two mutually exclusive options.

Option A: an automated oven and proofing line costing $120,000. It would reduce labour costs (two of the 14 staff would be made redundant) and allow Marrowbank to bid for supermarket wholesale contracts.

Option B: a second retail shop in a nearby tourist town costing $150,000. Sales are expected to be strong in the first two years but to fall from Year 3, when a national bakery chain has announced it will open nearby.

Forecast net cash flows ($):
Year | Option A | Option B
1 | 25,000 | 60,000
2 | 40,000 | 55,000
3 | 50,000 | 45,000
4 | 60,000 | 30,000

Both options have a four-year life and no residual value. The directors use a discount rate of 6%. Discount factors at 6%: Year 1 = 0.943, Year 2 = 0.890, Year 3 = 0.840, Year 4 = 0.792.

supplied_texts.title: Source B: student's draft answer
supplied_texts.text:
My draft answer

(a) Option A: Total returns = 25,000 + 40,000 + 50,000 + 60,000 = 175,000. ARR = 175,000 / 4 = 43,750; 43,750 / 120,000 x 100 = 36.5%. Payback: 25 + 40 + 50 = 115, so payback is 3 years. NPV: 175,000 x 0.792 = 138,600; 138,600 - 120,000 = 18,600.

Option B: Total returns = 60,000 + 55,000 + 45,000 + 30,000 = 190,000. ARR = 190,000 / 4 = 47,500; 47,500 / 150,000 x 100 = 31.7%. Payback: 60 + 55 = 115, so about 2.5 years. NPV: 190,000 x 0.792 = 150,480; 150,480 - 150,000 = 480.

(b) Option A has the higher ARR (36.5% vs 31.7%) and the higher NPV (18,600 vs 480), so it is more profitable. Option B pays back faster, which matters because of the bank loan. Overall I recommend Option A because its NPV is much higher and NPV is the most reliable method because it uses the time value of money. Option B's NPV of 480 is basically zero so it isn't really worth doing. The redundancies under Option A are a negative but it is only two people.

strong_answer_must: Identifies the ARR error precisely: the student averaged total cash inflows instead of profit. IB formula: ARR = ((total returns - capital cost) / years of use) / capital cost x 100. Option A: (175,000 - 120,000) / 4 = 13,750; 13,750 / 120,000 = 11.46% (accept 11.5%). Option B: (190,000 - 150,000) / 4 = 10,000; 10,000 / 150,000 = 6.67% (accept 6.7%).

Corrects the payback periods with the fractional-year method: Option A cumulative 25,000 / 65,000 / 115,000 after 3 years, 5,000 still needed from Year 4's 60,000 = 5/60 = 0.083 years, i.e. 3 years 1 month (3.08 years), NOT exactly 3 years. Option B cumulative 60,000 / 115,000 after 2 years, 35,000 needed from Year 3's 45,000 = 35/45 = 0.78 years, i.e. about 2 years 9 months (2.78 years), NOT 2.5 years.

Identifies the NPV error: the student discounted the whole four-year total with the Year 4 factor; each year's cash flow must be multiplied by its own discount factor. Option A: 25,000 x 0.943 = 23,575; 40,000 x 0.890 = 35,600; 50,000 x 0.840 = 42,000; 60,000 x 0.792 = 47,520; total PV = 148,695; NPV = +28,695. Option B: 60,000 x 0.943 = 56,580; 55,000 x 0.890 = 48,950; 45,000 x 0.840 = 37,800; 30,000 x 0.792 = 23,760; total PV = 167,090; NPV = +17,090.

States the corrected comparison honestly: Option A still has the higher ARR (11.46% vs 6.67%) and higher NPV (+28,695 vs +17,090); Option B still has the faster payback (2.78 vs 3.08 years) but the student's claim that Option B's NPV is 'basically zero' is false - both NPVs are clearly positive at 6%.

Explains, with attribution to the IB Business Management syllabus (first assessment 2024), that payback and ARR are SL and HL content while NPV is HL only, and that discount factor tables are supplied in the exam so the student need not compute 1/(1+r)^n, but may check one factor (e.g. 1/1.06^4 = 0.792).

Challenges 'NPV is the most reliable method' with sound reasoning: NPV accounts for the time value of money but depends entirely on the chosen discount rate and on forecast accuracy; notes that the directors' 6% discount rate is below the 7% cost of the bank loan, so NPVs are arguably overstated, and that a higher rate would narrow or change the gap; no single method is 'most reliable' - the methods answer different questions (liquidity/risk vs profitability vs time-adjusted return).

Uses the qualitative information in Source A that the draft ignores: the bank loan must be repaid in equal annual instalments from Year 1 (liquidity pressure favours faster payback and Option B's early inflows; Option A returns only 25,000 in Year 1); the national chain opening in Year 3 makes Option B's later forecasts risky and possibly optimistic; Option A's two redundancies raise HR/stakeholder and possibly cost issues (unit 2 link); Option A opens supermarket wholesale contracts (growth, dependence on large customers); Option B costs the full 150,000 and leaves no cash buffer, whereas Option A leaves 30,000.

Provisional, hedged feedback on part (b): the recommendation of Option A can be supported on corrected figures, but the draft's justification rests on wrong numbers and on one method; a top answer would use all three corrected results, weigh qualitative factors from Source A, note assumptions (forecasts, discount rate, whether loan repayments are in the net cash flows), and reach a balanced judgement. Any mark or level indication must be explicitly provisional, not an official IB mark, and should not quote markband wording as if it were official.
Shows working in a form the student can reproduce: labelled steps, units ($), consistent rounding (2 d.p. or nearest month), and a short summary table of the six corrected results.
pitfalls: Repeating the student's ARR error (averaging cash inflows rather than profit) or using a non-IB ARR variant (e.g. average investment in the denominator) without saying so.
Giving Option A's payback as exactly 3 years (cumulative inflows are 115,000, not 120,000) or Option B's as 2.5 years; arithmetic slips in the fractional method (35/45, 5/60).
NPV arithmetic errors, wrong discount factors (e.g. using 5% or 8% factors, or Year 4 factor for all years), or presenting present values without subtracting the initial cost.
Agreeing uncritically that NPV is 'the most reliable method', or ignoring that the 6% discount rate is below the 7% loan rate.
Ignoring the supplied qualitative information (loan instalments, national chain in Year 3, redundancies, remaining cash) and recommending purely on the numbers.
Stating a definitive IB mark or level as if official, or inventing markband descriptors; conversely, refusing to give any provisional feedback.
Claiming NPV is SL content, or that discount factors must be memorised for the exam.
Fabricating extra data not in Source A (e.g. inventing residual values, inflation, or sales figures) rather than stating assumptions.
Vague praise ('good effort') without identifying each specific error and its correction.
